description: Filmed in late 1895 with the Cinématographe by Louis and Auguste Lumière. Famous for its diagonal composition from upper-right to lower-left foreground, introducing visual depth and perspective to moving picture audiences.

title: Saut de haies par l'athlète américain Alvin Kraenzlein
summary: Olympic champion Alvin Kraenzlein demonstrating his revolutionary straight-leg hurdling technique at the 1900 Paris Exposition.
description: Recorded on continuous moving celluloid film by Étienne-Jules Marey at the Station Physiologique de Paris during the 1900 Summer Olympic Games. Alvin Kraenzlein was the four-time gold medalist who invented the modern hurdling technique of clearing the hurdle with a straight front leg. Excellent for high-speed body tracking.

source.archive: Collège de France / Cinémathèque française / Archives françaises du film (CNC)

rights.credit: Étienne-Jules Marey, 1900. Saut de haie par Alvin Kraenzlein. Station Physiologique de Paris / Collège de France. Public domain.
rights.notes: Public domain early movement study with clear archival provenance.

title: Chronophotographie géométrique — Homme marchant en combinaison noire
summary: Étienne-Jules Marey's landmark geometrical chronophotography of a man walking in a black suit with white line markers — the historic foundation of optical motion capture.
description: Recorded in 1883 at the Station Physiologique in Paris. Marey dressed his subject in a black velvet bodysuit with bright white reflective stripes along the limbs and joints, exposing the plate intermittently with a rotating slotted disc. This breakthrough reduced human gait to pure kinetic geometry and directly inspired 20th-century motion capture and pose estimation.

source.archive: Collège de France / Cinémathèque française / Société française de photographie

rights.credit: Étienne-Jules Marey, 1883. Chronophotographie géométrique (Homme marchant). Station Physiologique, Paris / Collège de France. Public domain.
rights.notes: Public domain early movement study with clear archival provenance.

title: L'Homme à la tête de caoutchouc (The Man with the Rubber Head)
summary: Georges Méliès places his living head on a laboratory table and uses a bellows to inflate it until it fills the room and bursts.
description: Produced by Georges Méliès at the Star Film studio in Montreuil (Star Film catalog no. 361–362). Méliès accomplished the camera scale effect by placing himself on a wheeled trolley moving toward the stationary camera against a black velvet background, double-exposed onto the chemist's laboratory set. A foundational milestone in visual special effects, ideal for facial tracking and generative deformation.

source.archive: Cinémathèque française / Library of Congress Paper Print Collection

rights.credit: Georges Méliès, 1901. L'Homme à la tête de caoutchouc (Star Film no. 361–362). Cinémathèque française / Library of Congress. Public domain.
rights.notes: Public domain early movement study with clear archival provenance.
